podcast.title: Release of "Sparkle" Movie (April 1976)
podcast.body: In April 1976, Warner Brothers released the movie "Sparkle," a film loosely based on the story of The Supremes. "In April of 1976, Warner Brothers released a movie called Sparkle, which was loosely based on the story of the Supremes."

podcast.title: Acquisition of Sire Records (1978)
podcast.body: Warner Brothers acquired Sire Records in 1978, incorporating the formerly independent label into a major label operation. This acquisition included artists signed to Sire at the time, such as the Talking Heads. "But when Sire was acquired by Warner Brothers in 1978, they became part of a major label operation."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Largest Record Company in 1988
podcast.body: In 1988, Warner Brothers was considered the largest record company in the world, and it was to this major label that R.E.M. transitioned from their indie label IRS. "Then in 1988, the group accepted an offer to jump from IRS. Their indie label, the one they'd been with from the beginning, to Warner Brothers, the largest record company in the world at the time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 3

podcast.title: Major Label Signing of R.E.M. (1988)
podcast.body: Warner Brothers signed R.E.M. in 1988 for an initial sum of $6 million after a bidding war, which was an exceptionally large amount for an indie band at that time. Eight years later, they renewed the deal for $80 million, signifying R.E.M.'s commercial success and influence in the music industry. "Warner signed them in 1988 for $6 million, an insanely huge number for an indie band at that time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 2: (90-81)

podcast.title: R.E.M. Signing (April 8, 1988)
podcast.body: Warner Brothers, a major record label, successfully signed R.E.M. on April 8, 1988, offering a significant $6 million check and a promise of complete creative control. This move was pivotal as R.E.M. became the largest college rock indie band to transition to a multi-million dollar major label, seeking expanded distribution and an end to their constant touring cycle. "So when Warner's came with that $6 million check on April the 8th, 1988, they signed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 8

podcast.title: Dispute with Linkin Park (2005)
podcast.body: Warner Brothers was involved in a public and contentious dispute with Linkin Park in 2005, occurring during a period of financial instability for the label. The label accused the band's management of "extortion" and "making baseless charges" in their negotiation tactics, while Linkin Park sought a $60 million advance. "executives were brawling with Lincoln Park, one of the label's biggest assets, and one of the label's biggest sources of revenue."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: R.E.M.'s Contractual Obligations Fulfilled (2010)
podcast.body: R.E.M. fulfilled their contractual obligations to Warner Brothers by 2010, after which they became free agents. This event marked a significant turning point in the band's career, leading to their eventual breakup when independent recording attempts stalled. "by 2010 they'd fulfilled their contractual obligations to Warner Brothers and became free agents."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Attempt to Sign Grimbey
podcast.body: Warner Brothers, a prominent record label, actively sought to sign Grimbey. They went as far as inviting the band members, who were young, around 22 years old, and without much money, to Disneyland for a day with all expenses paid, in an attempt to persuade them to sign. "una de esas importantes discográficas que fue Warner Brothers acabó invitándolos a Disneylandia para pasar un día allí para que ficharan por ellos."

podcast.title: Attracting Indie Bands
podcast.body: Warner Brothers successfully signed prominent indie bands like R.E.M., Husker Dü, Sonic Youth, and Nirvana by offering them significant contracts and the promise of wider distribution, stable income, and more sustainable touring conditions that independent labels could no longer provide. "So it came to pass on April 8, 1988, R.E.M. signed with Warner Brothers and took home a $6 million check."

podcast.title: Early Earth Wind & Fire Deal
podcast.body: Earth Wind & Fire initially signed with Warner Brothers Records, releasing two albums and a soundtrack with modest success before disbanding and moving to Columbia Records. "The group signed to Warner Brothers Records, and two EWF albums came and went, along with that Sweet Back soundtrack, to only modest success."

podcast.title: Financial Struggles (Mid-2000s)
podcast.body: In mid-2005, Warner Brothers faced significant financial difficulties, including new management, cost-cutting measures, layoffs of over 1,000 employees and 30% of its artist roster in 2004, and a negative credit rating due to debt. The label's attempt to raise $750 million through a stock offering was met with a hesitant market, achieving only $16 per share instead of the targeted $24. "Warner Brothers was under new management and was trying to cut both costs and raise money."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Initial Rejection of Linkin Park
podcast.body: Warner Brothers Records initially turned down Linkin Park (then known as Hybrid Theory) "many, many times" before eventually signing them, indicating their initial skepticism despite later success. "The label that finally took a chance in the band was Warner Brothers, even though they had told this band to go away many, many times."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Initial Rejections of Linkin Park
podcast.body: Warner Brothers Records initially turned down Hybrid Theory (later Linkin Park) at least three times before finally signing them in late 1999. This signing was largely due to a former Zomba A&R executive, Jeff, who had become a VP at Warner. "even though Warner had turned down Hybrid Theory slash Lincoln Park three times in the past, with this guy in charge, got named Jeff, they got a meeting, and they were signed in late 1999."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Instruction to Create Videos for MTV
podcast.body: Due to MTV's initial struggle to acquire enough video content, Warner Brothers, which owned numerous record labels, instructed its subsidiary labels to actively produce music videos. This directive aimed to ensure a steady supply of new material for the fledgling network. "And these labels were instructed to get on the video bandwagon so that MTV would have a steady supply of new products."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Jeff Blue's Role
podcast.body: Jeff Blue, who had initially championed the band at Zomba, later moved to Warner Brothers and became their internal advocate, ultimately securing Linkin Park's record deal. "their champion was, again, this dude Jeff Blue, who had quit Zamba and had moved over to Warner Brothers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Label's Misjudgment of Linkin Park's Sound
podcast.body: Despite Linkin Park's eventual success with over 100 million records sold, Warner Brothers Records was initially unsure how to market the band, with some, including the label president, reportedly disliking their sound and debating whether to release their debut album at all due to "screaming and rapping." They made various suggestions, such as cutting the rap, Mike Shinoda rapping like Fred Durst, bringing in a reggae vocalist, or adding gimmicks to Joe Hahn. "Warner did not know what to do with Lincoln Park and some, including apparently the president of the label just hated their sound."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Major Label Adoption of "New Wave"
podcast.body: Warner Brothers Records was one of the major labels that quickly adopted Seymour Stein's "New Wave" marketing term. This rapid embrace, alongside Polygram Records and other major labels by 1980, significantly contributed to establishing "New Wave" as a widely used, catch-all term for the diverse new music emerging in the post-punk era. "Seymour's marketing term was then picked up by Warner Brothers Records, and then by Polygram Records, and then other major labels."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Parent Company of MTV
podcast.body: Warner Brothers was the parent company of MTV, giving them significant influence over the early direction and content of the music television channel. "The good news is that the parent company of MTV, Warner Brothers, owned a lot of record labels."

podcast.title: Parent Company of Reprise Records
podcast.body: Warner Brothers was the parent company of Reprise Records, the label Grimbey eventually signed with. This connection meant that despite rejecting Warner Brothers directly, Grimbey ultimately became associated with the larger corporation through Reprise. "pertenecía Warner Brothers."

podcast.title: President Tom Wally's Meeting Style
podcast.body: Tom Wally, the president of Warner Brothers, demonstrated an unconventional approach to meeting Billy Talent. He insisted the band come to his New Jersey beach house rather than him coming to the city. During a "s***ly little session" in a rented airplane hanger, he sat and looked at the floor, preoccupied with his house. Despite the odd circumstances, he still wanted to sign them and later hosted them for dinner on his patio during a family birthday, providing fried chicken and beer. "Tom Wally had, he wanted to see us. He was the president of Warner Brothers. And he didn't want to leave his beach house in New Jersey to come to the city."

podcast.title: Rob Cavallo's Pivotal Role in Signing Green Day
podcast.body: Rob Cavallo, a representative for Warner Brothers, played a crucial role in signing Green Day to the label. Cavallo had a strong history of success, including helping to launch The Goo Goo Dolls, and his father had managed prominent groups such as The Lovin' Spoonful and Earth Wind & Fire. He famously signed Green Day for $300,000 without ever having seen them perform live. "But then a Warner Brothers rep named Rob Covello started some hard lobbying. He also had a pretty good track record."

podcast.title: Shareholder Threat Over Body Count's "Cop Killer"
podcast.body: During the controversy surrounding Body Count's song "Cop Killer," shareholders of Warner Brothers Records threatened to withdraw all their investments if the label did not address the band and the song. "It got so crazy that shareholders threatened to pull all their money for Warner Brothers records if the label didn't do something about Body Count."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Signing of Linkin Park
podcast.body: Warner Brothers eventually signed Linkin Park on their fourth attempt, despite the band having been rejected about four dozen times by various labels. Most within the label, apart from one persistent advocate, held low expectations for the band's potential success. "They were finally signed to Warner Brothers on their fourth try. They had been rejected three times, fourth try, they got in. No one at the label, with the exception of the guy who successfully begged his bosses to give the band a contract, thought that Lincoln Park would amount to anything."

srcs.episode: The 00's Part 3: The Return of Rock

podcast.title: Strategic Major Label Distribution for Indie Bands
podcast.body: Warner Brothers, a major label, engaged in a unique partnership with Rancid, an Epitaph band, by agreeing to distribute and "stealthily promote" their records. This allowed Rancid to maintain their punk rock ethics by staying with an indie label while benefiting from a major's reach. "but they agreed to have their epitaph records distributed and stealthily promoted by Warner Brothers, one of the majors."
